prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms brought optical frequency standards to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: Having read all eight opening ballots, I keep B061 first. The optical lattice clock is a measurement instrument in the strict sense: Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the lattice light shift so that many atoms can be interrogated at once, which is what allows the statistical gain and the fractional uncertainty near 10^-18. Every systematic (blackbody shift, lattice light shift, collisions, density shifts) has been identified and measured, and independent labs in Japan, the US, Germany, France and China have built clocks and compared them directly across continents. That is the reproducibility record I trust most among the candidates. The consequences are concrete and already realised: millimetre-to-centimetre relativistic geodesy, tests of the constancy of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches, and the basis of the roadmap for a redefinition of the second. Attribution is the cleanest on the list: Katori for the concept and first demonstrations, Ye for carrying strontium to the 10^-18 regime together with the many-body and cavity-based clock work. Five of eight members put it in their top three, and seven of eight proposed the identical two-name pair, so it is the one candidate where there is no real dispute about who should be named.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the field stands on prizes already given: Hall and Haensch (2005) for the frequency comb and Wineland and Haroche (2012) for single-quantum-system control and ion clocks. The committee may see an optical-clock prize as an incremental third step in one tradition, and the pending redefinition of the second means the headline application has not yet happened. Competing groups (Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemonde, Lisdat and others, plus the ion-clock groups) reached comparable accuracy, so a two-name prize draws a line through a contested field. I also note that by my own standards the discovery content is an engineering-physics achievement rather than a new phenomenon, which some colleagues weigh less heavily than a new state of matter.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B008 (Berry and Aharonov) first and places B061 sixth, calling it arguably slightly early because the redefinition of the SI second is still pending and the technology is still advancing, and noting that Hall and Haensch already received the 2005 prize for the comb.
responses.response: I disagree on timing. A clock is judged by whether independent laboratories reproduce and cross-compare it, and that has happened at the 10^-18 level; the redefinition is a metrological-committee decision with its own schedule and says little about the physics. Waiting for it would reward the administrative step rather than the demonstration. On the comb, the clocks use it, but the magic-wavelength lattice and the control of systematics are new and separate. I do agree with your point on B008: geometric phases are foundational and mature, and as an experimentalist I would only ask which measurement made the effects quantitative (Tonomura-type holography is not named in the credit), so I keep it below the clocks but do not regard it as weak.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B019 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) first as a new organising principle for quantum states, and puts B013 second, while ranking B061 only seventh although he judges the clock maturity as timely rather than premature.
responses.response: We agree on maturity, so the difference is what the prize is for. Your case for B019 is conceptually strong and confirmed by HgTe transport and ARPES, but it extends a topological-matter field the committee recognised in 2016, and the attribution is awkward because Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe realisation and are outside the credited names (you note this yourself). B061 has no comparable credit gap. I would ask you whether the 2016 precedent weakens B019 more than the Hall/Haensch precedent weakens the clocks; I think the clock tradition is more clearly a new measurement capability, while topological insulators are one more instance of a field already honoured.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B013 (magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene) first, arguing that the correlated insulator and superconductivity discovery is widely reproduced and that timing is good, and that the theory-plus-experiment trio is clean.
responses.response: This is the strongest competing case and I rank it high on impact. My reservations are about maturity and attribution, not originality: the pairing mechanism is still unsettled, sample dependence is a concern raised by Johansson, and the experimental credit leaves out Yuan Cao, who is the first author of the 2018 papers (you flag this too). I would like to hear from the condensed-matter members how stable the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction credit is against Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, since Mehlig raised that. If those points are settled, I could support B013 as the lead; for now I regard it as a plausible alternative and not a better-defined achievement than the clocks.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B009 (IceCube neutrinos) first as an instrument-driven discovery of a new messenger, and B061 third, respecting the control of systematics, with B013 second.
responses.response: I share your preference for instrument-driven discovery and I think IceCube is a genuine one. My concern is the one you identify yourself: it is a very large collaboration, so the two-name credit to Halzen and Spiering has to rest on instigation rather than analysis, and the source identification of the bulk flux is incomplete (the NGC 1068 and TXS associations are a handful of objects, from a single detector). Only Danielsson and Olsson besides you ranked it, so it has the narrowest support. The clocks have multiple independent instruments, which is the reproducibility test I would apply to both.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B018 (circuit QED) first and B034 (Cirac and Zoller) second, arguing that circuit QED is the platform for superconducting-qubit work, and that the 2025 circuit prize makes the topic a natural continuation, and ranks B061 third.
responses.response: I agree that B034 is deep and mature, and I ranked it fourth. Our difference is that the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes me cautious about a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon (Eriksson raises the same concern), and Wallraff, who carried out the 2004 experiment, is outside the credited trio of B018, which limits fairness of the credit. For B034 the experimental validation came from others, mostly Wineland and Haroche's recipients, and the theory is arguably already half-honoured, so I prefer the experimental measurement result.

uncertainties: Whether the committee views the optical clock as a third step in a tradition already prized in 2005 and 2012, or as a distinct achievement.
Whether limiting the credit to Katori and Ye leaves out Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom-type clock groups or the ion-clock groups to an extent that the committee finds unfair.
Whether the magic-angle graphene case (B013) is mature enough for this year given the unresolved pairing mechanism, since I cannot judge the condensed-matter details myself.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should count for or against timing.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B061 from my profile: I have no collaboration, institutional link or mentor connection to Katori, Ye or the clock groups. For completeness, I work on rare-earth-doped crystal quantum memories, which is relevant to B002 (light-matter quantum interfaces, where the rare-earth line is a named omission), and Lund and WACQT overlap with Chalmers through Johansson, which touches B018 and B034 only indirectly; I would recuse myself from any B002 deliberation concerning the rare-earth memory credit.
